# Spherical Harmonics Optimization

Also called: SH Optimization, SH Distillation, SH Vector Quantization, SH Degree Reduction

## Overview
Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting addresses the high memory footprint and computational cost associated with storing and evaluating high-degree SH coefficients for millions of Gaussian primitives. It encompasses techniques to reduce parameter count, accelerate rendering, and compress storage without significant loss in visual fidelity. What sets this family apart from general [3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details](9128-3d-gaussian-splatting-implementation-details.md) is its specific focus on the angular representation of color/appearance, distinct from geometric optimizations like [Sorting and Rendering Pipeline Optimization](12180-sorting-and-rendering-pipeline-optimization.md) or density control.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the SH coefficients $\mathbf{c}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{3(L+1)^2}$ associated with each Gaussian $i$, where $L$ is the maximum SH degree. The standard 3DGS representation uses $L=3$, resulting in 48 coefficients per Gaussian (16 per RGB channel). The core principle is that the full angular resolution provided by high-degree SH is often redundant or computationally expensive, allowing for reduction, quantization, or distillation.

The rendering equation for a pixel $p$ involves evaluating the SH basis functions $\mathbf{Y}(\omega)$ at the viewing direction $\omega$ and dotting with the coefficients:
$$
C(p) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \alpha_i \left( \sum_{l=0}^{L} \sum_{m=-l}^{l} c_{i, l, m} Y_{l, m}(\omega) \right) \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j)
$$
Optimization strategies modify the storage or computation of $c_{i, l, m}$ to reduce the cost of this summation or the storage of the vector $\mathbf{c}_i$.

## Subtopics

### [First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation](9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md)
Reduces SH degree from 3 to 1 to decrease parameter count and computation cost. It employs a teacher-student distillation strategy where a pretrained high-degree teacher guides a low-degree student, minimizing differences in rendered outputs (color and depth) rather than coefficient values directly. Choose this when rendering speed and storage are critical, and a pretrained high-quality model is available.

### [Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation](10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md)
Derives analytical Jacobians of the rendering pipeline with respect to camera pose $T_{CW} \in SE(3)$ using Lie algebra. It solves the numerical instability and overhead of automatic differentiation in SLAM/tracking. Choose this for pose optimization tasks where gradient accuracy and speed are paramount.

### [Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting](13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md)
Enables multi-view mini-batch training by implementing thread-efficient partial rendering and a 3D-space compatible D-SSIM loss. It reduces gradient variance compared to single-view training. Choose this when training stability and convergence speed are prioritized over single-view simplicity.

### [Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization](14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md)
Compresses SH coefficients by replacing per-splat vectors with indices into a shared learned palette. It reduces storage from gigabytes to tens of megabytes. Choose this when memory bandwidth and storage size are the primary bottlenecks, and minor lighting artifacts are acceptable.

### SH Degree Zero Optimization
Setting the maximum SH degree to 0 removes superfluous operations, improving training speed. In the original 3DGS code, features represented by SH coefficients with degree > 0 for color remain unchanged during training, making them useless [S1, unofficial]. Directly changing the max degree to 0 yields a 16.25% improvement; with specific code changes to delete superfluous operations, it yields a 16.57% improvement but increases CPU-GPU process time [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting method [Parent] uses third-order SH ($L=3$) to represent view-dependent color. Subsequent research identified inefficiencies in this representation. [S1, unofficial] observed that higher-degree SH coefficients for color often remain unchanged during training, suggesting redundancy. Other works introduced distillation [S2, unofficial] and vector quantization [S1, unofficial] to further optimize the angular representation for deployment and training efficiency.
